A lithium ion battery includes a positive electrode and a negative electrode, and a nanoporous or microporous polymer separator immersed in an electrolyte solution between the positive and negative electrodes. Also included is a chelating agent for complexing with transition metal ions during operation of the lithium ion battery without affecting movement of lithium ions through the separator. The chelating agent is: dissolving in an electrolyte solution; grafted to the polymer of the separator as a pendant substituent group; a binder material attached to the negative electrode and/or the positive electrode; coating the surface of the diaphragm; and/or coated on the surface of the negative electrode and/or the positive electrode. The chelating agent is selected from: an ion trap in molecular form selected from polyamines, thiols, and alkali metal salts of organic acids; an alkali metal salt functionalized polymer of an organic acid; a polymer functionalized with a nitrogen-containing functionality; two or more functionally functionalized polymers.

Lithium ion batteryTechnical Field

The present disclosure relates generally to lithium ion batteries.

Background

Secondary or rechargeable lithium ion batteries are used in many stationary and portable devices, such as those encountered in the consumer electronics, automotive, and aerospace industries. Lithium ion type batteries are popular for a variety of reasons including: relatively high energy density, a general lack of any memory effect when compared to other kinds of rechargeable batteries, relatively low internal resistance, and a relatively low self-discharge rate when not in use. The ability of lithium batteries to undergo repeated charge-discharge cycles over their useful life makes them an attractive and reliable source of electrical energy.

Disclosure of Invention

A lithium ion battery includes a positive electrode including a binder material, a negative electrode including a binder material, and a nanoporous or microporous polymer membrane immersed in an electrolyte solution operatively disposed between the positive and negative electrodes. One or more chelating agents are included in the battery to complex with the transition metal ions in a manner sufficient not to affect the movement of lithium ions on the nanoporous or microporous polymer separator membrane during operation of the lithium ion battery. The chelating agent is at least one of the following: dissolving in an electrolyte solution; grafted to a polymer of the nanoporous or microporous polymer membrane as a pendant substituent; operatively disposed within the aperture of the diaphragm; a binder material attached to the negative electrode; a binder material attached to the positive electrode; coating on the surface of the diaphragm; coating on the surface of the negative electrode; and coating on the surface of the positive electrode. The chelating agent is selected from: a molecular form of an ion trap selected from the group consisting of polyamines, thiols, and alkali metal salts of organic acids; an alkali metal salt functionalized polymer of an organic acid; a polymer functionalized with a nitrogen-containing chemical group; and polymers functionalized with two or more functional groups.

Detailed Description

Lithium ion batteries generally operate by reversibly transferring lithium ions between a negative electrode (sometimes referred to as an anode) and a positive electrode (sometimes referred to as a cathode). The negative and positive electrodes are located on opposite sides of a porous polymer separator that is soaked with an electrolyte solution suitable for conducting lithium ions. Each of the negative and positive electrodes is also operatively associated with or supported by its respective current collector. The current collectors associated with the two electrodes are connected, for example by means of a junction, to an interruptible external circuit which allows the current to pass between the electrodes by electrically balancing the relative migration of lithium ions. In addition, the negative electrode may include a lithium intercalation host material, and the positive electrode may include a lithium-based active material capable of storing lithium ions at a higher potential than the intercalation host material of the negative electrode. The electrolyte solution may contain a lithium salt dissolved in an aprotic nonaqueous solvent.

It has been found that lithium ion batteries are adversely affected by the dissolution of transition metal cations from the positive electrode, which leads to accelerated capacity fade and, therefore, to a loss of battery durability. The transition metal cations migrate from the positive electrode to the negative electrode of the battery, causing it to become "poisoned". In one example, the graphite electrode is due to spinel Li from the positive electrodexMn2O4Mn dissolved from active material+2、Mn+3Or Mn+4Poisoning by cations. For example, Mn+2Cations can migrate through the battery electrolyte and deposit onto the graphite electrode. Mn when deposited on graphite+2The cation may become Mn metal. It has been shown that relatively small amounts (e.g., 90ppm) of Mn metal can poison graphite electrodes and prevent reversible electrode operation, thereby adversely affecting the useful life of the battery. The adverse effects of Mn deposition on the negative electrode are significantly enhanced when the cell is exposed to temperatures above room temperature (e.g., above 40 ℃), whether the exposure occurs only during storage (i.e., simply at an open circuit voltage in a certain state of charge) or during cell operation (i.e., during charge, discharge, or charge-discharge cycles).

By incorporating examples of the chelating agents disclosed herein into a battery, poisoning of a lithium ion battery by dissolved transition metals from the positive electrode can be reduced or prevented. Chelating agents, alone or bound to polymeric or ceramic materials, complex with and trap transition metal cations (e.g., Mn cations) leached from the positive electrode of a lithium ion battery, thereby preventing their migration to the negative electrode and associatedThe battery performance is degraded. Any transition metal cation that can be trapped by an example of a chelating agent includes cations such as the following metals: manganese (e.g. Mn)+2、Mn+3、Mn+4) Iron (e.g., Fe)2+、 Fe3+) Chromium (e.g., Cr)2+、Cr3+) Cobalt (e.g., Co)2+、Co3+) Nickel (e.g. Ni)2+、 Ni3+、Ni4+) And/or vanadium (e.g., V)3+、V4+、V5+)。

In some cases, some previously identified transition metal cation chelating/trapping materials can be quite expensive. Examples of the present disclosure propose a new material that is less expensive while performing well to prevent transition metal cations from migrating to the negative electrode.

Examples of the chelating agents disclosed herein may be any one or combination of the following: dissolved or dispersed in an electrolyte solution; a material grafted to/tethered to the nanoporous or microporous membrane (e.g., as a pendant substituent group grafted into the membrane or onto the polymeric or ceramic material of the membrane); a binder material attached to the negative electrode; a binder material attached to the positive electrode; disposed within the open pores of the septum; coating on a surface of the separator; coating on the surface of the negative electrode; and/or coated on the surface of the positive electrode.

Suitable chelating agents include metal ionophores, as used herein, that are bound to a particular ion (e.g., Mn)+2Or other transition metal cations) while allowing lithium ions to pass through. Inside the cell, the chelating agent effectively traps unwanted metal cations while lithium ion movement across the nanoporous or microporous separator is not affected during operation of the cell. In an example, the chelating agent selectively complexes with unwanted metal cations, such as by immobilizing metal cations (e.g., Co) that may dissolve from the positive electrode into the electrolyte solution+2、Fe+2、Mn+2Etc.). The chelating agent thus acts as a metal cation scavenger that traps and immobilizes unwanted metal cations, thereby preventing the metal cations from passing through the electrolyte solution and reaching the negativeMigration of the poles. It will be appreciated that the chelating agent complexes less strongly with lithium ions (e.g., a single trapping site per hundred sites is complexed by Li as compared to the manganese cation+Cation occupancy) and therefore does not adversely affect the movement of lithium ions between the anode and the cathode.

Figures 1 to 3 show different examples of polymeric chelants disclosed herein.

In fig. 1, the polymeric chelating agent forms the lithium ion battery separator 16. In this example, the separator 16 itself is a porous film of polymeric chelating agent. In fig. 1, the polymer backbone is denoted by reference numeral 13, the chelating agent bound to the polymer backbone is denoted by reference numeral 15, and the pores in the film are denoted by reference numeral 17.

As shown in fig. 1, this example of the separator 16 has pores 17 formed throughout the polymer backbone 13. The chelating agent 15 is attached to the polymer backbone 13. In this example, the bonded chelating agent 15 is part of the membrane matrix and may be present inside the open pores 17. In examples of the present disclosure, free (molecular) chelating agents 15 (i.e., not bonded to a polymer) or polymeric chelating agents may also be used, for example, as filler materials within the membrane matrix and/or operatively disposed within the pores 17 of the membrane 16 (e.g., as microbeads (separate from the membrane matrix) within the pores 17 of the membrane 16).

In another example, the free (molecular) chelating agent 15 may also be dissolved or dispersed in the electrolyte solution.

Referring now to fig. 2, the polymeric chelant is in the form of a coating 24 on a nanoporous or microporous membrane 26. The coating 24 and the nanoporous or microporous membrane 26 together form another example of a lithium ion battery separator 16'. Since the coating 24 is formed on the surface of the nanoporous or microporous membrane 26, in some cases, some of the polymeric chelating agent may migrate into the pores 17' of the nanoporous or microporous membrane 26.

The polymeric chelant may be formed as shown in fig. 1, including chelant 15 attached to polymer backbone 13. The resulting coating 24 also includes pores 17. In examples where the membrane 26 is coated with a polymeric chelating agent, the polymeric chelating agent may be suspended in tetrahydrofuran, and this suspension may be deposited on the membrane 26 or otherwise exposed to the membrane 26. For example, a wet film of the suspension may be applied to the membrane 26.

Examples of suitable nanoporous or microporous membranes 26 include polyolefins. As an example, the polyolefin may be Polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), a blend of PE and PP, or a PE and/or PP porous film of a multilayer structure. Referring now to fig. 3, the polymeric chelant is in the form of a coating 24 on a structure 25. Coating 24 and structure 25 together form an example of positive electrode 14'. The coating 24 may also or alternatively be located on the negative electrode 12, for example, as shown in dashed lines in fig. 6. The structure 25 includes a lithium transition metal based active material 19, conductive carbon 21, and a binder 23. It should be understood that any lithium transition metal based active material 19 that is capable of adequately undergoing lithium intercalation and deintercalation while serving as the positive terminal of a lithium ion battery may be used. Binder 23 of structure 25 (or negative electrode 12) may be any polymeric binder capable of structurally holding lithium-based active material 19 together. Some examples of binder 23 include polyvinylidene fluoride (PVdF), Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) rubber, carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), lithium polyacrylate (LiPAA), sodium polyacrylate (NaPAA), sodium alginate, and/or lithium alginate. In an example, LiPAA and Na/Li alginate may be ideal for use in high voltage (5V) positive electrode materials.

Fig. 4-6 illustrate different examples of lithium ion batteries 10, 10', 10 "incorporating different examples of polymeric chelants disclosed herein. The battery 10, 10', 10 "generally includes an anode 12, a cathode side current collector 12a, a cathode 14, a anode side current collector 14a, and a separator 16, 16', or 26 positioned between the anode 12 and the cathode 14. It is to be understood that separator 16, 16', 26 and/or positive electrode 14 and/or negative electrode 12 may include a chelating agent 15 and a polymer backbone 13 coated thereon. Each example of the lithium ion battery 10, 10', 10 "also includes an interruptible external circuit 18 connecting the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14.

Referring now to fig. 4, the lithium-ion battery 10 includes a separator 16 disposed between the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14 as shown in fig. 1. As described above, the separator 16 is formed of an example of a polymeric chelating agent. A separator 16, which serves as a sponge and an electrical insulator for the electrolyte-containing solution, is sandwiched between the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14 to prevent physical contact between the two electrodes 12, 14 and the occurrence of a short circuit. The separator 16, in addition to providing a physical barrier between the two electrodes 12, 14, ensures that lithium ions (indicated in fig. 4 by black dots and open circles having a (+) charge) and associated anions (indicated in fig. 4 by open circles having a (-) charge) pass through the electrolyte solution filling its pores. The chelating agent 15 present in the matrix of the membrane 16 is also effective in trapping and immobilizing unwanted metal cations (e.g., Mn)2+) So as to prevent these metal cations from migrating through the electrolyte solution and reaching the negative electrode 12. In another example, the chelating agent 15 (not bound to the polymer) may be dissolved or dispersed in the electrolyte solution. Some examples of chelating agents in molecular form (one example of which is the tetrasodium salt of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTANA) are listed further below4))。

The negative electrode 12 may include any lithium host active material capable of sufficiently undergoing lithium intercalation and deintercalation while serving as the negative terminal of the lithium ion battery 10. Examples of lithium host active materials include graphite or low surface area amorphous carbon. Graphite is widely used to form negative electrode 12 because it exhibits good lithium intercalation and de-intercalation characteristics while being relatively inert and also can store lithium in amounts that produce relatively high energy densities. For example, commercial forms of Graphite that may be used to make the negative electrode 12 may be obtained from Timcal Graphite & Carbon (Bodiso, Switzerland), Lon Za Group (Basel, Switzerland), or Superior Graphite (Chicago, Ill.). Other materials may also be used to form the negative electrode including, for example, Lithium Titanate (LTO), silicon or silicon carbon composites, and tin oxide.

The anode 12 may also include a polymer binder material 23 mixed with the lithium host active material to structurally hold the lithium host active material together. Some examples of binders include polyvinylidene fluoride (PVdF), Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) rubber, carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC), sodium alginate, or lithium alginate. These materials (i.e., the lithium host active material and the binder) may be mixed with high surface area carbon (e.g., acetylene black) in order to ensure electron conduction between the current collector (shown as 12a in fig. 4) of the anode 12 and the active material particles. The negative side current collector 12a may be formed of copper or any other suitable electrically conductive material known to those skilled in the art.

The positive electrode 14 in the lithium ion battery 10 of this example is similar to the structure 25 described above in connection with fig. 3. In short, the positive electrode 14 may include any one of the aforementioned lithium transition metal-based active material 19, conductive carbon 21, and binder 23.

Adjacent to the cathode 14 is a cathode side current collector 14a, which may be formed of aluminum or any other suitable electrically conductive material known to those skilled in the art.

The negative side current collector 12a and the positive side current collector 14a may be positioned in contact with the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14, respectively, to collect and move free electrons to and from an interruptible external circuit 18 connecting the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14.

In one example, each of the negative electrode 12, the positive electrode 14, and the porous separator 16 is soaked in an electrolyte solution. It should be understood that any suitable electrolyte solution capable of conducting lithium ions between anode 12 and cathode 14 may be used in lithium ion battery 10. In one example, the electrolyte solution may be a non-aqueous liquid electrolyte solution comprising a lithium salt dissolved in an organic solvent or a mixture of organic solvents. Those skilled in the art are familiar with the types of lithium ion batteries 10 that may be used in such batteriesVarious non-aqueous liquid electrolyte solutions of (a) are also well known how to make them or obtain them commercially. Examples of the lithium salt that can be dissolved in an organic solvent to form a non-aqueous liquid electrolyte solution include LiClO4、LiAlCl4、LiI、LiBr、LiSCN、LiBF4、LiB(C6H5)4、LiCF3SO3、 LiN(CF3SO2)2(LiTFSI)、LiN(FSO2)2(LiFSI)、LiAsF6、LiPF6、LiB (C2O4)2(LiBOB)、LiBF2(C2O4)(LiODFB)、LiPF4(C2O4)(LiFOP)、 LiNO3And mixtures thereof. These and other similar lithium salts can be dissolved in a variety of organic solvents, such as cyclic carbonates (ethylene carbonate, propylene carbonate, butylene carbonate, fluoroethylene carbonate), linear carbonates (dimethyl carbonate, diethyl carbonate, ethyl methyl carbonate), aliphatic carboxylic acid esters (methyl formate, methyl acetate, methyl propionate), gamma-lactones (gamma-butyrolactone, gamma-valerolactone), chain ethers (1, 2-dimethoxyethane, 1, 2-diethoxyethane, ethoxymethoxyethane), cyclic ethers (tetrahydrofuran, 2-methyltetrahydrofuran), and mixtures thereof.

The electrolyte solution may also include various additives such as solvents and/or salts as minor components of the solution. Exemplary additives include lithium bis (oxalato) borate (LiBOB), lithium difluorooxalato borate (lidob), vinylene carbonate, monofluoroethylene carbonate, propane sultone, 2-propyn-ol-mesylate, methyl difluoroacetate, succinic anhydride, maleic anhydride, adiponitrile, biphenyl, ortho-terphenyl, bibenzyl, diphenyl ether, n-methylpyrrole, furan, thiophene, 3, 4-ethylenedioxythiophene, 2, 5-dihydrofuran, tris hexafluoroisopropyl phosphate, trihydroxybenzene, tetramethoxytitanium, and the like. Although the invention has been given with some examples, it should be understood that other additives may be used. When included, these additives may constitute from about 0.05% to about 5% of the composition of the electrolyte solution.

Other electrolytes may be used in place of the electrolyte solution. As examples, polymer electrolytes, ionic liquids, molten electrolytes, and the like may be used. Specific examples of some ionic liquids include 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis (fluorosulfonyl) imide, 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis (trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide, phosphonium bis (fluorosulfonyl) imide, triethylphosphonium bis (trifluoromethylsulfonyl) imide, triethylphosphonium (2-methoxyethyl) imide, and bis (trifluoromethylsulfonyl) imide. Although some examples have been given herein, it should be understood that other polymer electrolytes, ionic liquids, and eutectic melt electrolytes may be used.

The lithium-ion battery 10 may support a load device 22 that is operably connectable to the external circuit 18. When the lithium-ion battery 10 is discharged, the load device 22 receives a supply of electrical energy from the current through the external circuit 18. Although the load device 22 may be any number of known electrically powered devices, some specific examples of power consuming load devices include motors for hybrid or electric vehicles, laptop computers, cell phones, and cordless power tools. However, the load device 22 may also be a power generation device that charges the lithium ion battery 10 for energy storage. For example, the trend of windmills and solar panels to generate electricity variably and/or intermittently often results in the need to store excess energy for later use.

Lithium-ion battery 10 generally operates by reversibly transferring lithium ions between a negative electrode 12 and a positive electrode 14. In the fully charged state, the voltage of the battery 10 is at a maximum (typically in the range of 2.0V-5.0V); while in the fully discharged state, the voltage of the battery 10 is at a minimum (typically in the range of 0V-2.0V). In essence, the fermi levels of the active materials in the positive electrode 14 and the negative electrode 12 change during operation of the battery, and the difference between the two (also referred to as the battery voltage) also changes. The cell voltage decreases during discharge as the fermi levels approach each other. During charging, the reverse process occurs, with the cell voltage increasing as the fermi level is split. During battery discharge, the external load device 22 enables current to flow into the external circuit 18 in a direction that causes the difference between the fermi levels (and, correspondingly, the battery voltage) to decrease. The opposite occurs during battery charging: the battery charger forces current to flow into the external circuit 18 in a direction that causes the difference between the fermi levels (and correspondingly, the battery voltage) to increase.

At the beginning of discharge, the negative electrode 12 of the lithium ion battery 10 contains a high concentration of intercalated lithium, while the positive electrode 14 is relatively depleted. When the negative electrode 12 contains a sufficiently higher relative content of intercalated lithium, the lithium ion battery 10 can generate a favorable current through a reversible electrochemical reaction that occurs when the external circuit 18 is closed to connect the negative electrode 12 and the positive electrode 14. In this case, the establishment of a closed external circuit results in extraction of intercalated lithium from the negative electrode 12. The current through the external circuit 18 may be controlled and directed through the load device 22 until the level of intercalated lithium in the negative electrode 12 falls below an operable level or the power demand is eliminated.

By applying an external battery charger to the lithium-ion battery 10 to reverse the electrochemical reactions that occur during battery discharge, the lithium-ion battery 10 can be charged or recharged at any time after its available capacity is partially or fully discharged. An example multifunctional separator for a lithium ion battery is fabricated using a phase inversion technique with poly (ethylene-alt-maleic acid) dilithium salt as the functional filler material and PVdF-HFP copolymer as the inert matrix material. The benefits from such a functional separator can be traced back to three important functions performed by the P (E-alt-MALi2) material: chelating dissolved manganese ions, accommodating additional Li + ions and scavenging protons.
